When you call something exact, you mean it is perfectly correct, with zero error, zero deviation, and zero approximation. There is no "almost," no "roughly," no "about." It matches reality or a standard so perfectly that nothing needs to be added, removed, or adjusted.

Think of it this way: if you ask someone for the exact time and they say "around 3 o'clock," they have failed. But if they say "2:58 PM," that is exact — a specific, pinpoint answer that leaves no room for guessing.

"Exact" does two things at once:

1. It signals perfect correctness.
The information is not close to true — it is true, completely and specifically. No part of it is wrong, estimated, or left out.

2. It signals perfect specificity.
It is not a general or vague answer. It is this one, this number, this moment, this word — no other.

Together, these give "exact" its sense of strictness. When something is exact, you are saying: "This is IT — not more, not less, not close, but precisely and specifically THIS."

You can attach "exact" to almost anything that can be measured, described, or matched:

Numbers and measurements:

  • "Tell me the exact distance, not an estimate."
  • "The exact price is ₹847, not 'about ₹850'."
  • Here, "exact" means the number has not been rounded or guessed.

Words and quotes:

  • "Those were her exact words."
  • This means you are quoting someone word for word, not paraphrasing or summarizing. Not "she said something about leaving" — but the precise words she actually used.

Location and time:

  • "I need the exact address." (Not just the neighbourhood — the specific door.)
  • "At the exact moment the clock struck midnight..." (That very second, not shortly before or after.)

Copies and matches:

  • "This is an exact copy of the original document."
  • "The two signatures are an exact match."
  • Here, "exact" means there is no difference between the two things being compared — they are identical in every detail.

Requirements and instructions:

  • "Follow the exact instructions on the label."
  • "We need your exact measurements for the uniform."
  • Here, "exact" means you must follow or provide the information with full precision — no substitutions, no shortcuts.
The Contrast: What "Not Exact" Looks Like

The true power of a word becomes clear when you see what it is not. The opposite of exact is approximate — meaning close, but not perfectly correct.

When something is not exact, you signal it with words like:

  • about, around, roughly, approximately, nearly, almost, more or less, in the region of

Examples:

  • "About 200 people attended." → not exact; the real number could be 187 or 214.
  • "It takes roughly 30 minutes." → not exact; it could be 27 or 35.
  • "He said something like 'I don't care.'" → not exact; those might not be the real words.

When you swap "about" or "roughly" for exact, you are making a strong claim: I am telling you the precise, correct thing — not an estimate.

"To be exact" — used to sharpen or correct a number or fact you just said:

  • "I waited for two hours — one hour and fifty-three minutes, to be exact."

It signals: I know it precisely, and I want you to have the precise figure.

"The exact same" — meaning completely identical, with no difference at all:

  • "He made the exact same mistake again."

"The exact opposite" — meaning something that differs in the most total, perfect way possible:

  • "She did the exact opposite of what I told her."

"Exact change" — the precise amount of money, so no change needs to be returned:

  • "Do you have exact change for the bus?"

"An exact science" — a subject or field where results can be measured and predicted with perfect precision (mathematics, physics). When people say "cooking is not an exact science," they mean results vary and cannot always be perfectly predicted.

"An exact replica / an exact copy" — something reproduced with no detail missing or altered.

These words often appear near "exact," and it helps to know how they differ:

Accurate means close to the truth — errors are small or absent. An accurate statement may still be slightly imprecise, but it is not misleading. You can be accurate without being exact: "About 100 people came" might be accurate if 97 came, but it is not exact.

Precise means a high level of detail and specificity in measurement or description. A precise measurement gives you many decimal places. But precision without accuracy can still be wrong — "The answer is 3.141592" is precise; whether it is exact depends on whether it is truly correct.

Exact combines both: it is specific and perfectly correct. It is the strongest of the three. When something is exact, there is simply no gap between what is said and what is true.
A Deeper Sense: The Strictness of "Exact"

"Exact" carries a quiet strictness with it. It sets a standard of zero tolerance. When someone says "I want the exact figures," they are not asking you to try your best — they are telling you that guessing or rounding is not acceptable.

This is why "exact" often appears in contexts where mistakes have consequences:

  • Legal documents use exact wording because every word matters.
  • Scientists report exact measurements because an approximation could mislead.
  • Contracts specify exact dates because "around June" is not enforceable.

The word quietly communicates: "This matters too much to be approximate."

Exact (adjective): Perfectly correct and perfectly specific, with no errors, no rounding, no guessing, and no room for interpretation. Something exact matches reality (or another thing) completely — not closely, not nearly, but fully. It is the opposite of approximate, rough, or vague.
